items.followUp: What adaptations of villi help them absorb digested food efficiently?

rubric.why: Identifies villi and where they are found.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing villi as finger-like projections of the small intestine lining.

rubric.why: States the main function of villi.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that villi increase surface area for absorption of digested nutrients.

modelAnswer: Villi are tiny, finger-like projections of the inner lining of the small intestine.
They increase the surface area for absorption of digested food into the blood and lymph.

items.followUp: Describe the population level of biological organization and give an example.

rubric.why: Establishes that this level concerns an individual organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an individual living organism as the individual level.

rubric.why: Explains the organism's place in biological organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an individual organism is a basic unit of biological organization.

rubric.why: Recognizes that organisms at this level may differ in cellular complexity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that an individual may be unicellular or multicellular.

rubric.why: Gives a valid individual-organism example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example of one organism.

modelAnswer: An individual organism is a single living thing and is the individual level of biological organization.
It may consist of one cell, as in Amoeba, or many cells, as in a human or a plant.
An individual carries out the essential activities of life, such as nutrition, respiration, growth and reproduction.
Examples include one Amoeba, one human being or one plant.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and function of mitochondria, and draw a labelled diagram.

rubric.why: Identifies the enzymes that enable lysosomes to digest material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that lysosomes contain digestive or hydrolytic enzymes.

rubric.why: Describes the main digestive role of lysosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that lysosomes digest wastes, foreign material or worn-out cell parts.

rubric.why: Includes a key structural feature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the lysosome as a membrane-bound sac or vesicle.

rubric.why: Assesses the requested labelled drawing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognisable lysosome sketch and 1 mark for correctly labelling the membrane and digestive enzymes.

modelAnswer: Lysosomes are small, single-membrane-bound sacs in the cytoplasm.
They contain digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes.
These enzymes digest foreign material, cellular waste and worn-out cell parts.
Lysosomes are sometimes called the suicidal bags of the cell because their enzymes can digest the cell if released.

Diagram: Draw a circle about 4 cm in diameter to represent a lysosome; draw a second close, concentric circle for its membrane; label the outer boundary “single membrane” and the inside “digestive enzymes.”

items.followUp: Compare Kingdom Fungi and Kingdom Animalia by describing their main characteristics.

rubric.why: Tests the defining cellular organization of Monera.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that monerans are prokaryotic or lack a true nucleus, and 1 mark for stating that they are generally unicellular.

rubric.why: Includes the usual body organization of monerans.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Monera as generally unicellular.

rubric.why: Tests the cellular organization of plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that plants are eukaryotic and have a true nucleus.

rubric.why: Tests characteristic plant structures and nutrition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts, and 1 mark for photosynthesis/autotrophic nutrition.

modelAnswer: Kingdom Monera consists of prokaryotic organisms; their cells lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Monerans are generally unicellular; examples include bacteria.
Kingdom Plantae consists of multicellular eukaryotic organisms with a true nucleus.
Plant cells usually have cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll.
Most plants make their own food by photosynthesis and store it mainly as starch.

items.followUp: Explain the role of the Calvin cycle in photosynthesis and name its main inputs and products.

rubric.why: Identifies light capture as the start of the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that chlorophyll/photosystems absorb light energy.

rubric.why: Tests the splitting of water and oxygen release.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is split and oxygen is released.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP production during the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light energy is used to form ATP.

rubric.why: Identifies the reduction of NADP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that NADP is reduced to NADPH using electrons and hydrogen.

rubric.why: Assesses the requested diagram and its principal photosystems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a labelled light-reaction scheme showing the two photosystems in sequence; the scheme should also indicate electron flow and products for full credit across the answer.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in photosystems absorbs light energy.
In photosystem II, light energy excites electrons; water is split by photolysis to replace them, releasing oxygen and hydrogen ions.
The excited electrons pass along an electron transport chain, and their energy helps form ATP from ADP and phosphate (photophosphorylation).
Light excites electrons again in photosystem I; the electrons and hydrogen are used to reduce NADP to NADPH.
ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reactions; oxygen is released.
Diagram: On a horizontal line about 12 cm long, draw and label “Photosystem II” at the left and “Photosystem I” at the right, with an arrow between them labelled “electron transport.”

Above each photosystem draw a downward arrow labelled “light”; beside photosystem II show “H₂O → O₂ + H⁺ + e⁻”; beside the electron transport arrow show “ADP + Pi → ATP”; after photosystem I show “NADP⁺ + H⁺ + e⁻ → NADPH.”

items.followUp: Trace the path of blood through the heart and lungs, naming the valves it passes.

rubric.why: Tests the entry of deoxygenated blood into the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for tracing deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava to the right atrium.

rubric.why: Tests passage through the right side of the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing passage from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

rubric.why: Tests blood flow from the heart to the lungs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for tracing blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.

rubric.why: Tests return of oxygenated blood to the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for tracing oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

rubric.why: Tests exit of oxygenated blood from the heart to the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for tracing blood from the left atrium through the left ventricle and out through the aorta to the body.

modelAnswer: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae.
It passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it receives oxygen.
Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.
It passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aorta to the body.
The valves prevent the backward flow of blood.

items.followUp: Define a population and explain how it differs from a community.

rubric.why: Shows that a community includes more than one species or population.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a community consists of populations of different species.

rubric.why: Includes the shared location of a community.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that these populations live together in the same habitat or area.

modelAnswer: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same habitat at the same time.

items.followUp: Define a scientific theory and give one example from biology.

rubric.why: Tests the meaning of a scientific law as a general statement about nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a scientific law as a statement describing a consistent pattern or relationship in nature.

rubric.why: Requires a valid example of a scientific law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as the law of conservation of energy or the law of biogenesis.

modelAnswer: A scientific law is a general statement based on repeated observations or experiments that describes a consistent pattern or relationship in nature.
An example is the law of conservation of energy.
